question: During the Spanish Presidency of the Council, the use of all the languages recognised in the Spanish Constitution as official languages of the European Union was raised. I would therefore like to ask the following questions: 1.
Could details be provided on the logistical needs (in terms of the number of professionals, booths and technical changes) that are required to introduce a new official language?
Can the EU budget accommodate an increase in the number of official languages for translation and for use in the day-to-day running of the institutions?
What is the cost per page of translating official documents?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.4.2024) 1.

An assessment of the logistical needs to introduce a new official language would require input from all EU institutions and bodies and would depend on many factors concerning the language in question, including the concrete arrangements and infrastructures needed for its introduction, the ease of recruitment of staff1 for translation, interpretation, legal revision, and publications, and the availability of terminology databases.

If requested by the Council, which is the institution responsible for deciding the official and working languages of the EU institutions and whether to amend Regulation 1/1958, the Commission could coordinate a formal interinstitutional process to assess the needs.
This approach was followed in 2015, when the Commission prepared a legislative financial statement2 on the phasing-out of the Irish language derogation, based on input from other institutions.

For any new language, it should be borne in mind that the ways of working of the translation services have changed over the years, that there are specific needs for training and infrastructure as regards interpretation and that the situation of each language is specific in terms of available resources and translation needs3. 2. The current EU budget does not foresee funding for new official languages.

As budgetary authority, the European Parliament and the Council exercise jointly budgetary functions and decide on the size of the EU budget. If the addition of a language under Regulation 1/1958 were to be agreed by the Council, the budgetary authority could make the relevant adjustments to the EU budget. 3.

As regards the cost per page of officially translated documents, the Commission is not able to provide such information as the cost depends on a range of fixed and variable parameters such as cost of staff, information technology tools, training, language resources, and, where relevant, outsourcing.
1 The specialised university training required to have professionals of the quality level needed to work in the EU

institutions is the competence of Member States. 2 Council document 13839/15. 3 In December 2023, upon request from the Spanish Presidency, the Commission prepared a preliminary cost estimate of EUR 44 million per year for a ‘full regime’ of an added language (distributed to delegations in Council document WK 16458/2023). This estimate was based on the work done to calculate the costs of Irish becoming a full official language.
